data.content_ref: inline:The target's entire defense rests on the concept of 'test severity': the preference for better-corroborated theories is justified because they survived 'the severest possible tests.' Yet the target's own third countercondition concedes that the defense collapses 'if the definition of severe test relies on inductive assumptions about background knowledge' — and it does, inevitably. Determining which test is 'severe' for a given theory requires judging what would constitute a serious attempt to falsify it: which experimental setups are genuinely challenging, which instruments are reliable, which rival predictions matter. These judgments are formed from background knowledge — prior empirical findings accepted as reliable. But accepting prior empirical findings as reliable enough to calibrate test severity is an inductive inference: it assumes that past instrument calibrations, prior corroborated auxiliary theories, and established experimental regularities will continue to hold when used to judge the severity of a new test. Without this inductive scaffolding, 'severity' is epistemically ungrounded — one cannot distinguish a severe test from a trivial one without inductively trusting background knowledge. The target acknowledges this vulnerability as a countercondition but offers no derivation, mechanism, or defense showing how severity can be defined non-inductively. Since test severity is the load-bearing concept that distinguishes 'methodological preference' from arbitrary choice, the defense fails on the target's own terms: either severity is defined using inductively-acquired background knowledge (collapsing the anti-inductive stance), or severity cannot be defined at all (collapsing the methodological justification into arbitrariness). This objection is distinct from the prior two, which targeted the predictive use of corroboration for future action; this one targets the constitutive dependency of 'severity' — the concept that makes the defense work — on inductive background knowledge.
